newsitem.title: USA: American General to buy Home Beneficial.
newsitem.headline: American General to buy Home Beneficial.

text.p: American General Corp., one of the nation's largest diversified financial services companies, said Monday it agreed to acquire Home Beneficial Corp. for $665 million.

Houston-based American General, an aggressive buyer in the consolidating insurance industry, said shareholders of Home Beneficial can choose to be paid in either cash or common stock in the $39-a-share deal.
The news sent Home Beneficial stock up $8.6875 to $37.9375 on Nasdaq. American General lost 25 cents to $40 on the New York Stock Exchange.

The deal will be American General's third life insurance company acquisition in the past two years at a total cost of $2.2 billion. The company is among the nation's biggest life insurers on the basis of sales.

Wall Street analysts called the acquisition, expected to close at the end of March 1997, a smart move for American General, which is determined to grow its business in the tough "home service" segment of life insurance.
"Home service," traditionally sold by agents going door-to-door, refers to basic life coverage including burial benefits focused on lower middle class families.
The average size of a policy is only $5,000, and the business is often expensive to maintain, analysts said.

"The home-service market is an expensive-type business because it has small policies, small face amounts and small premiums," said Larry Mayewski, senior vice president of A.M. Best Co.'s life and health division.
"American General recognises that it's a very difficult market to grow, and one way to grow is through acquisition," said Mayewski.

"It's a very good strategic fit for American General's home service operation," said Michael Albanese, vice president of A.M. Best Co. "Strategically, it helps American General maintain their position in what otherwise is a slow-growth sector of the market."
New-business growth for home service companies has been in the low single digits at best, and in many cases is on the decline, said Albanese.

Virginia-based Home Beneficial is also a good geographic fit for American General, since the former is strong in the mid-Atlantic region while the latter's customer base is in the South and Southwest, said Albanese.
Another analyst said the deal looked good for American General's shareholders, but that profits in the company's home-service business was disappointing.
"The home-service business at American General is over-capitalised in order to maintain its AAA claims-paying rating," said Caitlin Long, analyst at Salomon Brothers Inc.
"Even though the move is good from the perspective of gaining economies of scale, it's still a low-return business within American General's corporate structure," she said.
But Long said she would nonetheless raise her American General earnings estimate by 5 cents a share to $3.55 in 1997 and $3.95 in 1998.
